prompt.context: Your client is a termite control company that provides solutions for eliminating termites from homes. Their current solution involves setting up baiting systems (a similar concept to mouse traps) — the baiting system consists of stations that are set up around the house to attract and kill termites. A competitor has come up with a new solution that involves liquid sprays for killing termites. They have just started selling this treatment.
prompt.question: How should the client respond to the competitor's new liquid spray product?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's current market share and scale?
clarifying_info.a: The client has 20% market share with 100,000 new installations per year.

clarifying_info.q: Will existing customers switch to the spray product?
clarifying_info.a: Assume existing customers will not switch. Some new customers perceive spray as a health risk — some will switch to spray, others won't, but exact percentages are unknown.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have the capability to produce the spray product?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the client has the capability to produce spray.

clarifying_info.q: Are the two systems equally effective?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the systems are equally effective at eliminating termites.

exhibits.title: Pricing By Channel
exhibits.shows: A two-column table comparing pricing for the Baiting System and the Spray System across two service types.

exhibits.title: Fully-Loaded Cost By Channel
exhibits.shows: A two-column table comparing fully-loaded costs for the Baiting System and the Spray System across two service types.

exhibits.title: Client Historical Retention Rates
exhibits.shows: A table showing the percentage of customers from year 0 who renew their subscription in each subsequent year, from Year 1 through Year 10.

framework: Understand the competitive threat: What is the spray product, pricing, and who is buying it?
Analyze relative profitability: Compare per-customer profit streams for baiting vs. spray over the customer lifetime
Account for customer retention: Apply historical retention rates to project expected annual profits
Assess startup/entry costs: Determine the cost and feasibility of the client entering the spray market
Evaluate strategic options: (1) Do nothing, (2) Compete head-on with spray, (3) Offer both products, (4) Differentiate/market advantages of baiting
Form a recommendation: Decide whether and how to enter the spray market based on the profit and competitive analysis

questions.prompt: Calculate the per-customer profit for the initial installation for each product.
questions.guidance: Candidate should subtract fully-loaded cost from price for each product. Baiting is the lower-margin product on installation; spray commands higher upfront margin.

math.setup: Profit = Price - Fully-Loaded Cost for each channel and service type.
math.answer: Baiting: $250 initial, $100/yr renewal. Spray: $400 initial, $50/yr renewal.

questions.prompt: Using the historical retention rates, calculate the expected annual renewal profit per original customer for each product over 9 years, and the cumulative profit.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply each year's retention rate by the annual renewal profit margin. A strong candidate notices that baiting's higher annual margin, combined with decent retention, generates more cumulative profit over the long run despite lower initial profit. Spray profit advantage from upfront margin erodes quickly.

math.setup: Expected annual renewal profit = annual renewal profit margin x retention rate for that year. Cumulative profit = initial profit + sum of all expected annual renewal profits to date.
steps: Year 0 (initial): Baiting=$250, Spray=$400; Cumulative: Bait=$250, Spray=$400
Year 1 (90% retention): Bait renewal=$100x0.90=$90, Spray renewal=$50x0.90=$45; Cumulative: Bait=$340, Spray=$445
Year 2 (80%): Bait=$100x0.80=$80, Spray=$50x0.80=$40; Cumulative: Bait=$420, Spray=$485
Year 3 (70%): Bait=$70, Spray=$35; Cumulative: Bait=$490, Spray=$520
Year 4 (60%): Bait=$60, Spray=$30; Cumulative: Bait=$550, Spray=$550
Year 5 (50%): Bait=$50, Spray=$25; Cumulative: Bait=$600, Spray=$575
Year 6 (40%): Bait=$40, Spray=$20; Cumulative: Bait=$640, Spray=$595
Year 7 (30%): Bait=$30, Spray=$15; Cumulative: Bait=$670, Spray=$610
Year 8 (20%): Bait=$20, Spray=$10; Cumulative: Bait=$690, Spray=$620
Year 9 (10%): Bait=$10, Spray=$5; Cumulative: Bait=$700, Spray=$625
math.answer: The two products break even on cumulative profit around Year 4 ($550 each). After Year 4, baiting generates more total profit per original customer. By Year 9, baiting yields $700 vs. spray's $625 — a $75 advantage.

questions.prompt: What are the strategic implications of the profit analysis?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate synthesizes: (1) Spray has a higher initial margin but much lower renewal margin; (2) Declining retention means renewal revenue diminishes over time; (3) Discounting future cash flows would further erode spray's apparent advantage since its extra profit is front-loaded; (4) The client's existing customer base will not defect; (5) Some new customers fear spray toxicity — the client can exploit this perception. Key insight: allowing spray to cannibalize baiting would shift profit reliance to renewals that shrink each year.

brainstorming.prompt: What messaging or positioning advantages does the client have for the baiting system over spray?

categories.name: Safety
ideas: Time-tested safety record (no chemical exposure in the home)
No health risk to children, pets, or food
Spray perceived as toxic by some customers — amplify this concern

categories.name: Efficacy
ideas: Baiting system has a long track record of effectiveness
Spray is a new, unproven product — unknown long-term efficacy

categories.name: Brand & Heritage
ideas: 'Your full-service termite eradication expert since 1925' positioning
Established trust and reputation vs. new entrant

categories.name: Service Model
ideas: Ability to offer both products provides customer choice
Ongoing relationship through annual renewals vs. one-and-done spray

recommendation: The client should equip its fleet for spray application to avoid ceding the spray market entirely, since startup costs are low/manageable and there is little downside risk to entry.

However, the client should actively market the advantages of the baiting system over spray — especially safety for families and food — while positioning itself as the full-service provider ('able to accommodate both applications').
The client should NOT allow spray to fully cannibalize baiting, as the profit analysis shows baiting generates more long-run profit per customer due to its higher annual renewal margin.
risks: If new customer perception shifts strongly toward spray, baiting revenue could erode faster than projected
Discounting future cash flows would further narrow the profit advantage of baiting over spray, potentially undermining the case for the current system
If the competitor prices spray more aggressively or improves it, the toxicity fear advantage may diminish
next_steps: Quantify the startup/entry costs for adding spray capability to the fleet
Run customer research to measure the strength and durability of spray toxicity perception
Model scenarios with different customer switching rates to stress-test the recommendation
Develop marketing materials highlighting baiting safety and the company's full-service positioning
